newsitem.title: USA: Doctors misread, misadvise on cancer test - study.
newsitem.headline: Doctors misread, misadvise on cancer test - study.

text.p: Doctors who order genetic testing for a condition that can lead to colorectal cancer often do not understand the test and fail to give patients proper counselling, a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine said.

The study by a team led by Francis Giadiello of the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore was released as doctors are getting more opportunities to use genetic testing as an early warning system for serious diseases such as cancer.
There has been concern such tests would be used improperly, and the Giadiello study suggests some fears may be warranted.

"Many of the physicians whom we interviewed did not recognise the limitations of the testing," the researchers concluded. "Almost one-third of the patients would have received an incorrect interpretation of the test" from their doctors.

The test used in the study was for familial adenomatous polyposis, which is caused by a genetic defect and leads to benign tumours in the colons and rectums of young adults. The condition invariably leads to cancer in people in their 50s.

The test is always accurate when genetic material from an affected family member is available to pinpoint the defect but it can give false reassurance to 20 percent of the people with the condition when that genetic material is not available.

To assess whether the doctors who ordered the test were using it appropriately, the laboratory doing the testing interviewed them by telephone to see if they knew how it worked, properly prepared their patients and knew how to interpret the results.
They found that only 19 percent of the 177 patients received genetic counselling before the test and in 83 percent of the cases the doctor failed to get the patient's written informed consent.

"Offering genetic counselling before the test and obtaining informed consent for testing are considered essential but neither was done in over 80 percent of the cases," they concluded. Even more importantly, they said, "in almost one-third of the cases the physicians' interpretation of the test results was incorrect and would have led to the misinforming of the patients."

Those doctors did not know that the absence of an already documented genetic mutation in the test might still indicate the presence of familial adenomatous polyposis. They also failed to understand how mutations, detectable when a family member with the condition is included in the test, can cause the disease.

"Since colorectal cancer develops in virtually all patients with this disorder," the Giadiello group said, doctors who fail to worry about a false negative result and fail to continue looking for signs of cancer could be setting the stage for "devastating consequences in the future."
The researchers also found that in 17 percent of the patients it was unclear that the test was warranted.

In an editorial in the Journal, Robert Veatch of Georgetown University in Washington questioned the methods of the Giadiello team, asking whether the doctors who were questioned about the test were told beforehand they were subjects in an experiment.

"We do not know whether they were told that the call was part of a systematic research project that might uncover embarrassing findings about their practices," Veatch said. He added that "it is striking that a study focusing on the lack of consent by patients should raise questions about the adequacy of the clinicians' consent."
